skills.name: Establish compatible operands
skills.definition: Prepare operands so subtraction can proceed directly by rewriting them into compatible forms, including finding common denominators, converting to equivalent fractions, and normalizing whole numbers or nonstandard mixed numbers.
skills.merge_rationale: S01 and S02 are both preparatory transformations applied before subtraction. In the dossiers, both serve the same problem-solving phase: making operands subtraction-ready. They are diagnostically close because both involve representation change rather than execution of subtraction.

skills.name: Subtract aligned parts
skills.definition: Carry out subtraction once operands are in compatible form, including subtracting numerators over a common denominator and subtracting whole and fractional parts separately.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because execution of subtraction is a distinct cognitive operation from preparation, regrouping, simplification, and final formatting.

skills.name: Regroup for subtraction
skills.definition: Borrow or regroup across whole and fractional parts when the fractional part of the minuend is insufficient for subtraction.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because borrowing produces a distinctive error pattern and is not always required. It has strong diagnostic value in mixed-number and whole-minus-fraction items.

skills.name: Simplify result
skills.definition: Reduce the resulting fraction or rewrite zero-valued fractional results into simpler equivalent forms.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because simplification is a finalization skill with its own common student errors and does not always co-occur with recombination.

skills.name: Compose final form
skills.definition: Recombine whole and fractional parts or present the result in its final mixed-number, fraction, or integer form.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because final answer composition is distinct from simplification; students may correctly compute parts yet fail to express the final form properly.

skills.name: Prepare operands for subtraction
skills.definition: Rewrite fractions, whole numbers, or mixed numbers into subtraction-ready forms by establishing common denominators, converting to equivalent fractions, or normalizing operands.
skills.merge_rationale: Inherited from the K=5 merge because these are both operand-preparation skills that occur before subtraction proper.

skills.name: Execute subtraction and regroup if needed
skills.definition: Subtract compatible whole and fractional parts, including borrowing or regrouping across parts when the fractional part is insufficient.
skills.merge_rationale: S04 is a conditional extension of S03 during execution: regrouping occurs only when ordinary subtraction of aligned parts is not directly possible. These skills are tightly linked in solution flow, especially in mixed-number subtraction, and can be meaningfully combined at a coarser level as the core subtraction process.

skills.name: Simplify result
skills.definition: Reduce the computed result to a simpler equivalent form, including reducing fractions and rewriting zero-valued fractions as 0 or an integer when appropriate.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because simplification remains a distinct post-computation operation with independent diagnostic value.

skills.name: Express final answer
skills.definition: Present the computed result in final form by combining whole and fractional parts or omitting zero parts as appropriate.
skills.merge_rationale: Kept separate because final expression of the answer is still distinguishable from simplification; a student may simplify correctly yet fail to compose the final mixed number or integer.

aggregation_notes: The main aggregation pattern follows natural phases of fraction-subtraction problem solving: preparation, execution, and finalization. For K=5, the two preparation skills (matching denominators and normalizing operands) were merged because both are representational setup steps that make operands subtraction-ready. Borrowing was preserved separately because it has distinctive error patterns and is not universally required. For K=4, borrowing/regrouping was merged with subtraction execution because regrouping is best understood as a conditional part of carrying out subtraction once operands are prepared. Simplification and final composition were not merged at either level because they remain diagnostically distinct: students often succeed at one and fail at the other.
